details.summary: The four levels of learning build from lowest to highest: Rote (repeat facts), Understanding (explain concepts), Application (use knowledge to solve problems / perform skills), and Correlation (relate knowledge across domains and adapt in new situations). Instructors should teach toward correlation, not stop at rote memorization.

details.summary: Stability is the tendency of an aircraft to develop forces (and moments) that restore it toward its original steady-flight condition after a disturbance. Distinguish static stability (initial tendency) from dynamic stability (behavior over time).

Lift rises with speed largely because relative wind hits the lower surface harder and more air mass is accelerated/deflected downward (Newtonian view). Dynamic pressure also rises with V², so the pressure difference across the wing grows. Same AOA, more speed → more lift — until you hit structural or stall limits.
The three aircraft axes (longitudinal, lateral, vertical) intersect at the center of gravity. Moments and stability are referenced to that CG point — which is why loading changes handling.

Adverse yaw on turn entry comes from aileron drag: the raised wing’s down-aileron makes more lift and more induced drag, while the lowered wing’s up-aileron makes less lift and less induced drag — so the nose yaws opposite the roll. Teach coordinated rudder with aileron from the start of the roll.

Correct: the wing’s angle of attack is greater as the rollout starts. In a coordinated steep turn you’re already loaded up (load factor rises with bank — ~1.4 G at 45°, 2 G at 60°), so both wings fly at a higher AOA than wings-level to make the extra lift. Rolling out, you lower the aileron on the inside (low) wing so it rises; that deflection adds lift and aileron drag. Because AOA is already high from turn loading, the same aileron deflection makes more drag than when you rolled in from near 1 G / lower AOA. Teach: roll-in = lower AOA → less aileron drag; roll-out = still high G/AOA → more aileron drag — so rollout often needs more coordinating rudder. Distractors about one wing traveling faster are overbanking ideas, not this effect.

links.label: PHAK — Turns / Adverse Yaw / Load Factor

details.summary: To increase turn rate and decrease turn radius at the same time: steepen the bank and decrease airspeed. Rate ↑ with bank and with lower speed; radius ↓ with bank and with lower speed (within stall/load-factor limits).

Spin entry after a full stall: the down-going wing stays stalled while the rising wing unstalls and produces some lift — that lift asymmetry drives autorotation. Teach stall + yaw → spin; recovery starts with reducing AOA and stopping yaw.

Center of pressure is the point on the airfoil through which the net aerodynamic lift (pressure force) acts. It moves with AOA and is not the same as CG — the relationship between CP and CG drives pitching moments.

By definition, lift is the net aerodynamic force perpendicular to the relative wind; drag is parallel to the relative wind. Weight and thrust (or tow force) are separate. Teach students to resolve forces in the relative-wind axes, not the horizon axes, when analyzing climbs and glides.

Angle of incidence is the fixed angle between the wing chord line and the aircraft longitudinal axis — built into the airframe, not changed by the pilot. Do not confuse with angle of attack (chord vs relative wind), which the pilot does change.

Angle of attack (AOA) is the angle between the chord line and the relative wind. AOA — not pitch attitude or airspeed alone — is what the wing “sees.” Stalls occur at a critical AOA regardless of indicated airspeed.

The mean camber line runs from leading edge to trailing edge, equidistant from the upper and lower surfaces. The chord line is the straight line LE→TE. Camber is the curvature between those two lines; more upper camber is typical on glider airfoils.

Bernoulli’s principle (as taught in FAA materials): faster airflow over the curved upper surface lowers static pressure on top of the wing, contributing to lift. Pair this with the downward deflection / Newton explanation — both are part of the complete lift picture.

Wings produce lift from a pressure difference: relatively higher (positive) pressure below and lower (negative) pressure above the wing. That net force is perpendicular to the relative wind. Teach both pressure distribution and downwash as one story.

Bank misfiled under weather (aerodynamics). At zero geometric AOA the upper surface can still have pressure below atmospheric because of camber/flow acceleration — lift is about pressure difference, not “nose-up attitude.”

Induced drag is the drag created as a byproduct of producing lift (wingtip vortices / downwash). It changes strongly with airspeed — roughly inversely with V² in level flight — so it dominates at slow speeds near the stall.
Above L/Dmax speed in level flight, total drag rises mainly because parasite drag increases with speed (≈ V²). Induced drag is falling, but parasite drag grows faster past the L/Dmax “bucket.”

Below L/Dmax speed in level flight, total drag rises because induced drag increases sharply as airspeed drops (higher AOA to hold level flight). That is the backside of the drag curve — important for slow flight and approach energy management.

Profile drag (a form of parasite drag) includes skin friction from air viscosity along the wing surface plus form drag from the airfoil shape. It rises with airspeed and is not the lift-induced component.

Induced drag varies inversely as the square of the airspeed (in steady level flight, roughly). Double the speed → about one-fourth the induced drag. Parasite drag does the opposite — varies with the square of speed.

In a coordinated turn, total lift tilts; the vertical component must still equal weight for level flight. As bank increases, vertical lift decreases unless you increase total lift (back pressure / higher load factor). In a glider, if you do not add enough, you sink faster — bank ↑ → vertical component ↓ → sink rate ↑.

Center of pressure (CP) is where the net aerodynamic force acts on the wing. As CP moves with AOA/configuration changes, pitching moments change — affecting aerodynamic balance and how much control input you need (controllability).

To turn, you must change the direction of lift (bank) so a horizontal component pulls the flightpath around. Rudder alone yaws; elevator alone pitches. A coordinated turn is bank + appropriate pitch + rudder to stay coordinated.

AOA directly controls how pressure is distributed on the wing (upper-surface suction and lower-surface pressure). Change AOA and you change that distribution — and therefore lift, drag, and pitching moment — before airspeed has time to catch up.

details.summary: A wing stalls at a critical angle of attack, independent of airspeed. You can stall at high speed (accelerated stall) or low speed — what matters is exceeding critical AOA. Weight, G-load, and CG change the stall speed, not the stalling AOA.

Critical (stalling) angle of attack depends on wing design (airfoil, planform, devices) — not on weight or airspeed. Weight and CG change stall speed; they do not change the stalling AOA of that wing configuration.

In ground effect, at the same AOA as out of ground effect, lift increases and induced drag decreases because the surface interferes with wingtip vortices / downwash. That is why float on landing happens — the ship “keeps flying” in the cushion.

Bank misfiled under weather (aerodynamics). Flying in ground effect just clear of the surface can be sustained at a slightly lower airspeed than out of ground effect because the ground interferes with wingtip vortices / downwash, reducing induced drag.

In severe turbulence, slow to maneuvering speed (VA) or less. VA is the maximum speed at which full control deflection will not overstress the airframe — your turbulence penetration airspeed reference.

A stall occurs when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack — regardless of airspeed, attitude, or power. Any flight attitude can stall if AOA is high enough; “slow = stall” is incomplete teaching.

On the standard total-drag vs airspeed curve (Figure 20), point A at the bottom of the bucket is L/Dmax — maximum lift/drag ratio in steady flight. That speed is the key reference for best glide performance in still air.

On the same drag curve, the airspeed at L/Dmax (often labeled point B depending on the figure edition) gives maximum glide range in still air. Best endurance / minimum sink is a slower speed; do not mix those two up on the oral.

Spiral instability comes from strong static directional stability combined with weak dihedral effect. A small bank → nose yaws into the turn (strong weathercock) → outer wing speeds up → bank steepens into a spiral dive. Dihedral/roll stability is what should fight that.

Positive dynamic stability is the most desirable: after a disturbance, oscillations damp out and the airplane returns to equilibrium. Positive static but negative dynamic means it starts back then oscillates worse — not what you want.

Static instability means that when disturbed from steady flight, the aircraft develops forces that take it farther from the original condition (initial tendency is divergent). Contrast with positive static stability (restoring tendency).

Positive static stability (longitudinal): after you push the elevator forward and release, the nose initially tends to return toward the original pitch attitude. Initial restoring tendency = positive static stability.

Negative static stability: after a pitch disturbance (elevator forward and release), the nose initially moves farther from the original position. Divergent initial tendency — undesirable for a training glider.

Maneuverability is the quality that lets an aircraft be operated easily and withstand the stresses of flight maneuvers. It is about how readily and safely you can change attitude / flightpath — related to, but not the same as, controllability.

Controllability is the capability of an aircraft to respond to pilot control inputs, especially regarding flightpath and attitude. Soft or heavy controls, CG position, and speed all change how controllable the ship feels.
Neutral static stability: after elevator forward and release, the nose stays at the new attitude — no restoring and no divergent tendency. Contrast with positive (returns) and negative (keeps going).

In a longitudinal phugoid oscillation, airspeed and pitch trade back and forth while angle of attack stays nearly constant. It is a long-period energy exchange (kinetic ↔ potential), not a short-period AOA hunting mode.

Positive static stability with negative dynamic stability produces divergent oscillations — the airplane initially returns toward equilibrium but each swing grows larger. You want positive static and positive (damped) dynamic stability.
Wing dihedral increases lateral (roll) stability: when a wing drops, the lower wing meets the relative wind at a higher AOA and produces more lift, rolling the aircraft back toward wings-level.
Aspect ratio = wingspan ÷ mean chord. High aspect ratio (long, skinny wings) is typical of sailplanes and reduces induced drag at a given lift.

High aspect-ratio wings (long, narrow) typically stall at a lower airspeed than low aspect-ratio wings of similar area — more efficient lift at a given AOA, lower stall speed. Gliders exploit this; expect different handling vs short-wing trainers.
At constant velocity, a high aspect-ratio wing has less drag than a low aspect-ratio wing — especially at high AOA — because induced drag falls as aspect ratio rises.
Figure 21 aspect-ratio table: highest AR is the largest span/chord ratio — keyed aircraft 3. Compute AR ≈ span ÷ average chord for each row.
Figure 21: lowest aspect ratio is keyed as aircraft 4. Short span relative to chord → low AR → more induced drag.

Holding other factors constant, the highest aspect-ratio wing (aircraft 3 on Figure 21) generates the greatest lift efficiency / greatest lift in the bank’s framing — high AR wings are more efficient producers of lift for a given area/AOA regime.
Figure 21, other factors constant: lowest aspect-ratio wing (aircraft 4) generates the greatest drag — induced drag rises as AR falls.

Glider airfoils generally have greater camber on the upper surface than the lower surface (positive camber). That shape favors upper-surface acceleration and pressure difference for efficient lift at soaring AOAs.

A slight upward (negative) flap deflection reduces camber and typically decreases drag — used on some sailplanes for high-speed cruise / interthermal runs. Down flaps increase camber, lift, and drag for thermaling or landing.

In a turn, the inward (horizontal) component of lift is opposed by centrifugal force. In a steady coordinated turn those horizontal forces balance; lift’s vertical component balances weight (level turn) or not (climbing/descending turn).
At 60° of bank in a coordinated level turn, load factor is 2 G — the resultant of weight and centrifugal force equals twice the glider’s weight. Memorize: 60° → 2 G; 45° → 1.4 G.
Spoilers’ primary purpose on gliders is to decrease lift (and increase drag) so you can steepen the approach without a large airspeed increase. Teach approach control with spoilers, not “dive flaps.”

A spin has at least one wing stalled (autorotation). A steep spiral does not — both wings are flying, airspeed and G rise, and the spiral can exceed VNE/load limits. Differentiating spin vs spiral is a core CFI teaching point.

details.summary: Maximum gliding distance (still air) occurs at L/Dmax, which is where induced drag equals parasite drag — the bottom of the total-drag curve. Fly that speed (adjusted for wind/sink as needed) for best range.
Best L/D occurs when parasite drag equals induced drag. That identity is the same idea as “bottom of the drag bucket” — useful as a memory hook on the written.

The best L/D ratio itself is essentially constant with weight — a heavy glider flies the same L/Dmax number, but at a higher airspeed. Weight changes the speed for best L/D, not the ratio value (ignoring Reynolds-number nuances).

Adding ballast/weight: best L/D ratio stays about the same, but the airspeed for that glide ratio increases. Heavy = same glide angle at a higher speed (better penetration, worse low-speed climb in weak lift).

details.summary: Figure 38 glide problem: L/D 20:1 at 40 MPH. Altitude needed at B equals height to cover remaining distance at that glide ratio plus the 800 ft AGL arrival over C (no sink). Keyed answer 4,320 feet AGL — work distance÷20 then add 800.
Best glide speed (L/Dmax) gives the longest distance / longest cross-country glide in still air. Minimum sink maximizes time aloft, not distance.

details.summary: Northern Hemisphere magnetic compass: acceleration on east or west headings makes the compass indicate a turn toward the north (ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South). Use this when teaching compass errors on climb/descent entries.
Acceleration/deceleration errors are negligible on north or south headings — the compass indicates correctly while speeding up or slowing down on N/S. Errors show on E/W headings (ANDS).

Magnetic deviation is compass error from local magnetic fields in the aircraft — metals, electronics, speakers, etc. It is unique to each airplane/installation and is corrected with a compass correction card.

Rolling out to south with a magnetic compass (Northern Hemisphere): start rollout after the compass passes south by about (latitude − normal rollout lead) degrees. Southerly turns are lead/lag reversed from northerly turns — overshoot south, undershoot north.

From a south heading, rolling into a standard-rate right turn (Northern Hemisphere): the compass indicates a turn to the right but faster than the actual turn (leads). UNOS memory aid: Undershoot North, Overshoot South when rolling out.
Deviation varies with heading on the same aircraft — that is why the compass card lists corrections by heading blocks. Variation is geographic; deviation is airframe/heading-dependent.
Pitot-static system errors are generally greatest at low airspeed (high AOA / large position-error regime). Airspeed and altimeter can both be less trustworthy near the stall.

A clogged pitot tube affects the airspeed indicator (impact pressure). Static-only instruments (altimeter, VSI) are unaffected unless the static system is also blocked. Teach partial-panel implications for gliders with limited backup.

Cold air is denser: in colder-than-standard temperatures you are lower than the indicated altitude (true altitude < indicated). “From high to low, look out below” applies to both pressure and temperature. Critical for mountain / winter ops.

Never replenish an aircraft oxygen system with industrial oxygen — contaminants and moisture can be hazardous. Use only aviators’ breathing oxygen. (Bank answer text is truncated/OCR-noisy; the teaching point is aviation-grade O₂ only.)

The oxygen system most commonly found in light GA aircraft is continuous flow (cannula or mask with continuous delivery). Diluter-demand and pressure-demand systems are more typical of higher-performance / high-altitude aircraft.
Replenish aircraft oxygen systems with aviation (aviators’ breathing) oxygen only — not medical or industrial grades sold for other uses.

A total-energy compensator reduces climb/dive (stick-thermal) errors on the variometer caused by airspeed changes — so the vario better reflects air-mass vertical motion rather than zoom climbs and pushovers.

A total-energy compensator makes the variometer respond primarily to air-mass vertical motion (up/down currents), not to stick-induced climbs/dives. TE probes sense pitot + static so pitch-driven altitude changes are largely cancelled.
In a continuous-flow oxygen mask, the rebreather bag stores exhaled oxygen-rich gas so you can re-inhale part of it — helping conserve the oxygen supply.
VNO (maximum structural cruising speed) is marked as the upper limit of the green arc on the airspeed indicator (also the lower limit of the yellow arc). Do not confuse with VNE at the red line.
Maximum structural cruising speed (VNO) is color-coded — upper end of the green arc / bottom of the yellow arc. VNE is the red line; VA is not color-coded.
Maneuvering speed (VA) is an important limitation not shown by color coding on the ASI. It changes with weight and must be memorized from the POH/placards.

Density altitude from Figure 24: use pressure altitude (from elevation + altimeter setting) and OAT on the DA chart. For 5,515 ft / 30°C / 29.40 in Hg the keyed DA is about 8,750 feet. Hot + low pressure = high DA.
Figure 24 DA problem: elevation 3,795 ft, OAT 24°C, altimeter 29.70 → keyed density altitude about 5,750 feet. Convert to pressure altitude, then apply temperature on the DA chart.
Figure 24: elevation 3,450 ft, 35°C, 30.40 in Hg → keyed DA about 5,950 feet. Hot day still drives DA up even with a high altimeter setting.

Density altitude rises when temperature rises, moisture increases, and pressure decreases (hot, humid, low-pressure day = high DA). High DA means less performance: longer ground roll, poorer climb, higher true airspeed for a given IAS.
At a given airport, an increase in air temperature increases density altitude (air less dense). High DA hurts takeoff/climb performance.
With pressure and temperature constant, higher humidity makes air less dense → longer takeoff distance and reduced climb. Water vapor displaces heavier dry-air molecules.
CG is computed along the longitudinal axis (fore-aft station). Lateral imbalance matters operationally, but standard W&B worksheets solve for the longitudinal CG location in inches from datum.

details.summary: CG = total moment ÷ total weight. Moment is weight × arm. Add all weights and all moments, then divide. Same formula for gliders with pilot, ballast, and optional water.

links.label: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook

details.summary: CG aft of the aft limit: pitch stability is reduced and stall/spin recovery can become difficult or impossible. Never fly outside the weight-and-balance envelope — especially aft.
Highest stalling speed occurs with high gross weight and a forward CG. Heavy + forward CG means you need more lift (higher AOA sooner / higher speed) and the wing/tail combo stalls at a higher IAS.
CG at the aft limit (vs forward): lowest stalling speed, highest cruise performance, and least stability. Forward CG is more stable but stalls sooner and needs more elevator for flare.

Moving CG from aft limit to beyond the forward limit decreases cruising speed and increases stalling speed. Forward CG means more download on the tail (more trim drag) and a higher stall speed — sluggish and nose-heavy.

links.label: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook

details.summary: Exceeding the forward CG limit produces higher stalling speeds and more longitudinal stability (very stable but heavy elevator, hard flare). Aft of limits does the opposite: lower stall speed feel, less stability, easier to stall/spin.

Bank answer looks swapped. As CG moves aft, the aircraft becomes less stable (more sensitive in pitch, easier to stall/spin). Forward CG increases stability but raises stall speed and can make flare harder.

A forward CG is most critical on landing — higher stall speed, heavier elevator forces, and a harder flare / higher risk of wheelbarrowing or hard touchdown. Takeoff with forward CG is also sluggish but landing is the classic “most critical” answer.

As CG moves rearward, stall recovery becomes progressively more difficult — less nose-down pitching moment available and less static stability. Emphasize this when teaching loading and spin awareness.
CG too far aft can allow a flat spin — high rotation rate, nose-high attitude, and recovery that may be delayed or impossible. Aft loading is a spin-risk multiplier.
Mountain airport landings: expect higher true airspeed for a given IAS and longer landing distance because of high density altitude. Plan a longer rollout and go-around options.

Bank answer looks wrong: most weather occurs in the troposphere, not the tropopause. The tropopause is the lid; the weather layer is the troposphere beneath it. Study the troposphere for fronts, clouds, and turbulence.

The Sun is the primary driving force of Earth’s weather — uneven solar heating drives circulation cells, pressure systems, and fronts. Everything else (Coriolis, terrain, moisture) modifies that energy engine.
Standard average lapse rate in the troposphere used on many FAA questions: about 2 °C per 1,000 feet (≈ 3.5 °F/1,000 ft). Actual lapse rate varies and determines stability.
The most common ground-/surface-based temperature inversion is from terrestrial radiation on a clear, relatively calm night — ground cools, air near the surface becomes colder than air above.
Beneath a low-level inversion with high relative humidity, expect smooth air and poor visibility from fog, haze, or low clouds — pollutants and moisture are trapped under the lid.
Density altitude is found by correcting pressure altitude for nonstandard temperature. Pressure altitude first (29.92), then temperature correction → DA.
Standard sea-level values: 59 °F (15 °C) and 1013.2 mb (29.92 inHg). These are the ISA baseline for performance and altimetry teaching.
Wind is caused by pressure differences — air moves from high toward low pressure, then is turned by Coriolis and modified by friction near the surface.
Flow around a low is cyclonic (counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere). Highs are anticyclonic (clockwise NH).

Bank answer text looks swapped (vortex wording). Concept for the stem: winds at 5,000 feet more southwesterly while surface winds are more southerly mainly because surface friction slows and backs the wind near the ground; above the friction layer the wind is closer to geostrophic / gradient balance.
A low-pressure area or trough is associated with rising air (and often clouds/precipitation). Highs/ridges favor sinking air and clearer conditions.
As relative humidity increases, the temperature–dewpoint spread decreases. Small spread → closer to saturation → higher fog/cloud potential.
Relative humidity is the ratio of water vapor actually in the air to the maximum that could exist at that temperature (saturation).
Virga: precipitation that falls from a cloud but evaporates before reaching the ground. Often a dry-air / evaporative-cooling cue under the base.
Atmospheric stability is determined from the ambient (environmental) lapse rate compared with dry/moist adiabatic rates — steep lapse → unstable; shallow/inverted → stable.
Whether lifted moist air forms mostly stratiform or cumuliform clouds depends on the stability of the air being lifted — stable → layer/stratus; unstable → cumulus/showers.
Cumuliform cloud-base estimate (°F): (temperature − dewpoint) ÷ 4.4 × 1,000 ≈ feet AGL. Here (77 − 53) / 4.4 ≈ 5,500 feet AGL.
Cumuliform cloud-base estimate (°C): (temperature − dewpoint) × 400 ≈ feet AGL. Here (33 − 15) × 400 = 7,200 feet AGL.
Very stable moist air forced up a mountain slope tends to form stratus-type clouds with little vertical development and little or no turbulence — orographic layer cloud, not towering cumulus.
Middle-cloud bases in middle latitudes are commonly about 6,500 to 23,000 feet. Know low / middle / high families for icing and weather briefing vocabulary.
Nimbostratus: middle-level (often thickening) rain/snow/ice-pellet producer that can pose a serious icing hazard when temperatures are near or below freezing — continuous precip, not showery CB.
Unstable air is normally associated with good visibility (except in blowing sand or snow), cumuliform clouds, and turbulence — contrast with stable air’s haze and stratiform layers.
A moist, unstable air mass: cumuliform clouds and showery precipitation (plus turbulence and good visibility outside showers).
Advancing warm front with moist, unstable air: cumuliform clouds, turbulent air, and showery precipitation — not the classic stable warm-front stratus/drizzle pattern.

Bank answer looks swapped. Moist cold air being warmed from below becomes unstable (cumulus, turbulence, good visibility outside precip) — “restricted visibility” is the usual stable-air cue. Know the contrast for the checkride even if the key is noisy.
Stable air characteristically brings restricted visibility (haze, fog, smoke trapped in a layer) plus stratiform clouds and smooth air.

Bank Q/A garbled (OCR mix of humidity-spread wording with a thunderstorm answer). Strong updrafts and cumulonimbus are signatures of deep moist instability — not of an increasing temperature–dewpoint spread with rising RH (that statement is false).
Typical stable air-mass weather includes continuous (steady) precipitation from layered clouds — contrast with showery precip in unstable air.
Moist warm air being cooled from below becomes more stable — expect smooth air (and often stratiform cloud/fog potential), not towering cumulus.
Frontal waves normally form on slow-moving cold fronts or stationary fronts — the wave can amplify into a mature cyclone with warm and cold fronts.
Cool air moving over a warm surface is heated from below → instability and showers (and often good visibility between showers).
Wave on a stationary front oriented east–west across the U.S.: portion east of the wave normally becomes a warm front; portion west becomes a cold front — classic open-wave cyclone geometry.

Bank stem truncated. Over hills/ridges, expect the worst downdrafts/turbulence on the leeward (downwind) side — especially when flying into the wind toward the ridge lee. Stay upwind or high enough to clear rotor/sink.

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Ridge / Mountain Flying

details.summary: Low-level wind shear with a sudden direction change can occur with a low-level temperature inversion and strong winds above the inversion — classic morning shear under a nocturnal inversion.
Bank stem truncated (strong wind above an inversion). Expect wind shear and possible sudden airspeed loss when climbing or descending through the inversion top — brief hard, add approach margin.
Thunderstorm life cycle: beginning of rain at the surface marks transition into the mature stage (updraft + downdraft). Cumulus = updrafts; dissipating = mostly downdrafts.
Tornadoes are most likely with steady-state thunderstorms associated with cold fronts or squall lines — not ordinary air-mass “pulse” storms.
Cumulus stage of a thunderstorm: continuous updrafts (little or no precipitation at the surface yet). Bank stem has OCR bleed from mountain-wave text — answer is still continuous updrafts.

Bank stem OCR-mashed (mountain-wave statements mixed with CB/funnel wording). Correct pick for the mountain-wave true statements is typically 2 and 3: waves develop in a series on the lee side; humid large-amplitude waves show lenticulars at the crests. Use the Figure / handbook diagram, not the scrambled stem alone.
A squall line is usually associated with a fast-moving cold front — a narrow band of intense thunderstorms ahead of or with the front.

Hail hazard true statements (bank): large hail with strong updrafts + high liquid water; hail usually in the mature stage; hailstones can be thrown outward for several miles. Visual appearance alone is a poor hail predictor; hail can exist outside the cloud core downwind of the anvil.
Hailstones may be thrown outward from a storm cloud for several miles — clear air beside a CB is not automatically hail-safe, especially under/near the anvil.
Hail as an in-flight hazard is most likely associated with cumulonimbus clouds — avoid by wide margins; do not plan to “skirt” under the anvil.
Hail is most likely to be encountered beneath the anvil of a large cumulonimbus — ice is lofted in the updraft and falls out downwind under the anvil.
Fog needs high relative humidity (near saturation) plus a cooling or moistening process. Without moisture near saturation, fog does not form.
Radiation fog: high humidity in early evening, cool clear night, light wind, and favorable topography (valleys/drainage). Calm traps the cold layer; too much wind mixes it out.
Advection fog forms when moist air moves over a colder surface — common along coasts and with warm air over cool water/ground.
Advection fog can appear suddenly day or night and is typically more persistent than radiation fog — wind that would clear radiation fog often sustains advection fog.
Warm fronts commonly bring precipitation-induced fog — rain evaporates into cool stable air ahead of the front, saturating the layer.

Bank stem/answer look swapped. Warm-front fog is typically from warm moist air overrunning cooler air / saturation by evaporation and cooling. Separately: excellent soaring can exist in the cold air ahead of a warm front — that is a soaring-front teaching point, not the fog mechanism.

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Weather for Soaring

details.summary: Cold-front passage often leaves clear, unstable, dry air behind it — excellent soaring for hours to days. Warm-front weather is usually poorer for thermals (stable, moist, layered cloud).

Mountain-wave formation favors a stable layer near mountaintop height and a wind of at least about 15–25 knots blowing roughly perpendicular across the ridge — plus increasing wind with height in many setups.

Bank answer looks swapped (thermal/sun wording). Near mountains, the greatest danger from strong vertical/rotor currents is usually on the downwind (lee) side — rotor, turbulence, and sink. Stay upwind or well clear of the lee rotor zone.

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Mountain / Wave / Rotor

details.summary: One of the most dangerous mountain-wave features is severe turbulence in and below lenticular clouds (rotor zone). Lenticulars mark the wave; the rotor under them can destroy aircraft.

Bank stem text looks mis-pasted (mentions thermal indices), but the choices/key test dust-devil technique: avoid the clear area at the outside edge of the dust column because of severe downdrafts. Dust marks the rising core; the clear rim is often where air sinks hard. Teach students to treat that clear collar as a no-go, not a “cleaner” entry.

When soaring in a dust devil, an important precaution is to avoid the eye (core) of the vortex because of extreme turbulence. Dust may look inviting as a thermal marker, but the center can be violently turbulent. Prefer the smoother lift on the outside of the rotating column and leave immediately if the ride gets rough.
One of the best visual thermal markers is a smooth cumulus with a concave (domed-up / scooped) base — active feed from below. Ragged, decaying tops/bases are weaker.

Sea-breeze convective circulation forms because land absorbs and radiates heat faster than water. By day the land heats, air rises over land, and cooler air flows inland from the water; at night the pattern can reverse (land breeze).

Bank key points to steep escarpments/cliffs as a favored place for convective circulation to develop (strong differential heating / slope lift). Broader teaching: convection needs a heat source and unstable air — cliffs and sun-facing slopes often trigger early thermals.
In stable weather (poor thermals), you can still soar on the upwind side of hills/ridges with moderate wind — ridge lift. No sun-driven convection required if the wind hits the slope.
METAR Figure 3: calm wind is coded 00000KT. On the supplement, KDAL reports 00000KT — that is the calm station. Teach students to read wind group first in every METAR.

links.label: FAA Aviation Weather Handbook / METAR decoding

details.summary: METAR remarks encode precipitation begin/end. At KAUS, RAB25 means rain began at 25 minutes past the hour; duration to observation time is reckoned from that remark — keyed answer is 26 minutes for this figure set. Always decode RMK begin/end times.

METAR true set per bank: FG only with visibility < 5/8 SM; BR from 5/8 up to 6 SM; no provision for partial obscurations in that older keying. (Modern decoding still: know FG vs BR thresholds; VV is treated as ceiling in current practice — bank item 1 may be outdated.)
Ceiling is the AGL height of the lowest broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC) layer (not SCT). On Figure 3, KDAL’s OVC009 is the lowest ceiling among the stations — 900 feet AGL overcast.
(Figure 3) Read KAUS temperature and dewpoint from the METAR/surface report in the figure; the spread is temperature − dewpoint = 4 °C. Use the Figure pill for the actual print.
For KBRO on Figure 3, the reported ceiling is the lowest BKN/OVC layer — keyed as 25,000 feet (OVC250). Remember sky cover heights in METARs are hundreds of feet AGL (250 = 25,000).

For a brief summary of fronts, pressure systems, and circulation patterns, use Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) on aviationweather.gov. It replaced many old prog-chart workflows for that quick synoptic picture.
An individual microburst seldom lasts longer than about 15 minutes from the time the burst strikes the ground until dissipation. Brief but severe — plan avoidance, not “ride it out.”

Maximum downdrafts in a microburst may reach about 6,000 feet per minute. That vertical rate is unsurvivable near the ground in light aircraft/gliders — recognize virga, blowing dust, and storm outflow early.
Maximum-intensity winds in an individual microburst typically last only 2 to 4 minutes. Short peak, high damage potential — another reason to delay launch/landing when outflow is nearby.

If a nontowered airport lies inside Class D/C of a towered airport, two-way radio with ATC is required for landing clearance at the tower-controlled airport and to transit that controlled airspace — not for the satellite field’s pattern by itself when outside that requirement.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.129 / § 91.130 — Class D / Class C operations

details.summary: VFR operations in Class B are allowed for solo student pilots if they meet the specific Part 61 training/endorsement requirements for that Class B airspace. Class B is not “instructors only” — students can go with the right endorsement and equipment/clearance rules.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.95 — Operations in Class B airspace / at airports

details.summary: Operating in Class B requires two-way radio communications and a Mode C transponder (encoding altimeter) plus ADS-B Out when required by § 91.225. You also need an ATC clearance to enter Class B.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.131 — Operations in Class B airspace

details.summary: VFR flights are prohibited in Class A airspace. Class A (generally 18,000 MSL to FL600) is IFR only unless a specific authorization applies.

In Class E, basic VFR visibility goes from 3 SM to 5 SM when you are more than 1,200 feet AGL and at or above 10,000 feet MSL (with the matching cloud-clearance change to 1,000 ft above/below and 1 SM horizontal).
Class D normally extends from the surface up to and including about 2,500 feet AGL (charted as an MSL ceiling). Always read the dashed-blue number on the chart — individual airports vary.

Bank misfiled under weather (VFR cloud clearance). In controlled airspace more than 1,200 feet AGL and below 10,000 feet MSL, VFR minimum horizontal distance from clouds is 2,000 feet (also 500 below / 1,000 above).
Class G, more than 1,200 feet AGL and at or above 10,000 feet MSL: remain 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 1 mile horizontal from clouds (plus 5 SM visibility).
Class E VFR, more than 1,200 feet AGL and at/above 10,000 MSL: flight visibility required is 5 SM. Below that altitude band, Class E basic VFR is usually 3 SM.
Within the contiguous U.S., the floor of Class A airspace is 18,000 feet MSL (up to and including FL600, excluding some areas). Altimeter setting 29.92 in Class A.
With certain exceptions, Class E extends upward from 700 or 1,200 feet AGL to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL (the Class A floor). Magenta/blue vignettes show where the Class E floor starts.

Another Class E vertical-limit phrasing used on the test: Class E goes up to, but not including, the base of the overlying controlled airspace (e.g., a Class B/C shelf). Both “to 18,000” and “to overlying controlled” appear depending on the question’s wording.
Class C diagram (Figure 47): surface area (inner circle C) normally has a 5 NM radius. Memorize the standard Class C template: 5 NM surface / 10 NM shelf / ~20 NM outer area (when charted).

links.label: 14 CFR Part 71 — Designation of Class A, B, C, D, and E

details.summary: Class C shelf area (circle A on Figure 47) normally has a 10 NM radius. Shelf floor/ceiling are charted in the figure boxes — do not assume every Class C is identical; confirm on the chart.
On the Class C figure, box 2 is the base of the shelf area — keyed as 1,200 feet AGL for that diagram. Always read the figure’s altitude boxes; real Class C shelves vary by airport.

Class C Figure 47: box 1 is the vertical extent (ceiling) of the surface and shelf areas — keyed as 4,000 feet above the airport for that diagram. Always read the figure altitude boxes; real Class C tops vary.

Minimum avionics for Class C: two-way radio communications and a transponder with automatic altitude reporting (Mode C). Establish two-way comm before entry; ADS-B Out also applies in the Mode C veil / rule airspace where required.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.130 — Operations in Class C airspace

details.summary: Departing a satellite airport inside Class C without a tower: contact ATC as soon as practicable after takeoff. Establish two-way comm promptly; you cannot linger without talking.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.130 — Operations in Class C airspace

details.summary: All operations within Class C must be in an aircraft with a Mode C transponder (automatic altitude reporting), unless otherwise authorized. Two-way comm is also required to enter/operate there.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.130 — Operations in Class C airspace

details.summary: Do not fly through a restricted area unless you have prior authorization from the controlling agency. Restricted areas contain hazardous activities; permission is not optional.

A warning area is airspace of defined dimensions from three nautical miles outward from the U.S. coast. Hazardous activities to nonparticipating aircraft may exist — similar in purpose to a restricted area, but over international waters.
An MOA is established to separate certain military training activities from IFR traffic. VFR is not prohibited, but IFR traffic may be rerouted when the MOA is active.
When operating VFR in an MOA, exercise extreme caution if military activity is being conducted. Check NOTAMs / FSS for MOA status and monitor published frequencies when possible.
Flight through an MOA is permitted anytime (no clearance required for VFR), but use caution because of military activity. Contrast with restricted areas, which require authorization.

Military training routes with operations at or below 1,500 feet AGL use a four-digit number (IR#### or VR####). Routes mostly above 1,500 feet AGL use three-digit numbers. Charted on IFR/VFR charts — brief them on cross-countries.
A military airport rotating beacon is green and dual-peaked white (green-white-white). Civil lighted land airports are white-green; water airports white-yellow; heliports white-yellow-green.
Runway numbers 8 and 26 mean the runway is oriented approximately 080° and 260° magnetic. Numbers are magnetic course to the nearest 10°, with leading zeros dropped (08 → 8).
Standard practice: inbound to a nontowered airport, continuously monitor the appropriate CTAF from about 10 miles out. Announce position/intentions and fit into the flow.

links.label: AIM 4-1-9 — Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers

details.summary: At an airport with no tower, FSS, or UNICOM, broadcast intentions on the MULTICOM frequency 122.9 MHz. Use Chart Supplement CTAF when published; 122.9 is the default MULTICOM.
Segmented-circle Figure 54: traffic-pattern indicators show left-hand for Rwy 35 and right-hand for Rwy 17. L-shaped indicators next to the circle show pattern direction for each runway end.

With the wind cone in Figure 54, use the runway most nearly into the wind and the pattern shown by the indicators — keyed as left traffic on Rwy 35 or right traffic on Rwy 27. Wind sock + segmented circle together select runway and pattern.

Wake turbulence wingtip vortices circulate outward, upward, and around each wingtip. From behind the generating airplane, each vortex is a horizontal tornado that sinks and drifts with the wind. Knowing the circulation direction helps you picture where the hazard sits relative to the flightpath.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Bank answer text looks swapped (takeoff-behind-jet wording). Concept for the stem: a light crosswind (about 5 kt or less) can drift the upwind vortex over the runway and hold it in the touchdown zone longer — so a light crosswind is not “safe,” it can make wake more persistent for the following aircraft.

Departing behind a large jet: minimize wingtip-vortex hazard by becoming airborne before you reach the jet’s flightpath (rotate prior to the jet’s rotation point / liftoff path), then turn clear of the wake. Remaining below the jet’s path keeps you in the sinking vortices; extending the roll past the jet’s rotation point puts you into the vortex trail.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Landing behind a large jet: plan to touch down beyond the jet’s touchdown point so you stay above the sinking vortices. Avoid the “same aim point” that puts you in the wake.

Helicopters in forward flight generate wingtip-like vortices similar to fixed-wing aircraft (plus strong rotor downwash when hovering or at low speed). Do not teach “helicopters only make downwash.” Also remember vortices sink below the generating aircraft’s path after a short time — they do not stay level indefinitely.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: ATC provides a minimum of 6 miles separation for a small aircraft landing behind a heavy jet (wake turbulence separation). Still fly beyond the touchdown point and stay above the path.

links.label: AIM 7-3-9 — Wake Turbulence Separation for Arrivals

details.summary: Parachute jump site information is in the Chart Supplement (formerly Airport/Facility Directory). Check notices for jump aircraft frequencies and altitudes before overflying.

While a Flight Instructor Certificate is suspended, the holder may not apply for any rating to be added to that certificate during the suspension period. Suspension freezes upgrade/add-on applications on that certificate.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.19 — Duration of pilot and instructor certificates
14 CFR Part 61 — Certification: Pilots, Flight Instructors

details.summary: Under 14 CFR 61.15, a conviction for any federal or state offense involving the growing, processing, manufacture, sale, disposition, possession, transportation, or importation of narcotic drugs, marijuana, or depressant or stimulant drugs or substances is grounds for suspension or revocation of any certificate, rating, or authorization issued under Part 61. Related alcohol/drug motor vehicle actions also trigger reporting and certificate action rules in 61.15.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.15 — Offenses involving alcohol or drugs

details.summary: Student Pilot Certificates issued after April 1, 2016 have no expiration date. Solo and other privileges still require current instructor endorsements (e.g., 90-day solo) even though the plastic certificate itself does not expire.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.19 — Duration of pilot and instructor certificates
14 CFR § 61.87 — Solo requirements for student pilots

details.summary: A Flight Instructor Certificate expires 24 calendar months after the month of issue or renewal. Renew via FIRC, practical test, or other § 61.197 methods before expiration.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.197 — Renewal requirements for flight instructor certification

details.summary: To act as PIC of a glider using aerotow, you must have received ground and flight training on aerotow procedures/operations and an authorized instructor endorsement certifying proficiency (§ 61.31).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.31 — Type rating requirements, additional training, and endorsement requirements

details.summary: Minimum documentation to take an FAA knowledge test for any flight instructor rating is proper identification. (FOI/knowledge prerequisites differ from practical-test endorsements — this item is about the testing-center ID rule.)

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.35 — Knowledge test: prerequisites and passing grades
FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Authorization Matrix

details.summary: If the Administrator finds cheating or an unauthorized act on a knowledge test, that person may not take another knowledge test for 1 year (and certificate action may also apply).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.37 — Knowledge tests: cheating or other unauthorized conduct

details.summary: Cheating on a knowledge test can result in suspension or revocation of any certificate or rating held by that person — not just a retest delay.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.37 — Knowledge tests: cheating or other unauthorized conduct

details.summary: The instructor’s written endorsement that the applicant is prepared for a practical test must be dated within 60 calendar days preceding the date of application (14 CFR 61.39).
Under 14 CFR 61.39, an applicant for a practical test must have passed the required knowledge test within the preceding 24 calendar months (when a knowledge test is required).
If a practical test is not finished in one day, all remaining increments must be satisfactorily completed no later than 60 calendar days after the date the test began (14 CFR 61.43).

An aircraft furnished for a practical test must have no prescribed operating limitations that prohibit its use in any required area of operation (and meet the other Part 61 aircraft requirements). If the POH/placards forbid a required task, that ship cannot be used for that checkride task.

After a second knowledge-test failure, with training and an authorized instructor endorsement, the applicant may retest immediately — there is no mandatory calendar wait beyond getting the endorsement.

After a second practical-test failure, the applicant may retest after the examiner receives a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who gave additional training. There is no mandatory wait calendar day — keyed eligibility is the same day (January 13) once the required endorsement/training is done. Know 61.49.
After a first knowledge-test failure, retest requires an endorsement from an authorized instructor certifying additional training was given and the applicant is competent to pass the test.

A CFI applicant must demonstrate spins (airplane or glider, as appropriate) when being retested for deficiencies in instructional proficiency on stall awareness or spins from the initial test — not as a routine extra on every retest for unrelated items.

links.label: 14 CFR Part 61 — Flight Instructor Practical Tests

details.summary: After a second practical-test failure, the applicant may retest after receiving the necessary instruction and an endorsement from the authorized instructor who gave that training.
All flight training, flight-simulator training, and ground training time used toward a certificate/rating must be certified (endorsed/logged) by the instructor from whom it was received.

A commercial pilot must log the flight time necessary to meet recent flight experience requirements (and other required records). You do not have to log every flight for fun — but you must be able to show currency and qualification when exercising commercial privileges.
A flight review is not required if, within the required period, the pilot completed a pilot proficiency check conducted by the FAA (among other § 61.56 exceptions such as certain practical tests).
A standard flight review consists of a minimum of 1 hour of ground training and 1 hour of flight training (glider has an alternate three-flight option in § 61.56).
Without a current flight review (or qualifying substitute), a pilot may not act as PIC — including solo. Instructors who are also pilots need a current flight review to exercise PIC privileges.
Glider flight review: at least 1 hour ground instruction and either 1 hour of flight training or three instructional flights each including a flight to traffic-pattern altitude (§ 61.56).

After a permanent address change, you may exercise certificate privileges for 30 days before written notice to the FAA Airmen Certification Branch is required — then privileges stop until notified (§ 61.60).
Notify the FAA in writing of a permanent address change within 30 days. After 30 days without notice, you may not exercise pilot/instructor privileges until the change is filed.

A person seeking a private pilot glider rating is exempt from the knowledge test if they already hold a powered-aircraft rating (airplane, rotorcraft, etc.) — § 61.105 / glider private knowledge exceptions.
Minimum age for a Student Pilot Certificate limited to glider operations is 14 years (§ 61.83). Solo glider privileges also require the appropriate endorsements and training.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.83 — Eligibility requirements for student pilots

details.summary: Required solo endorsement: within the preceding 90 days, an authorized instructor endorses that training was given in the make/model to be flown and the student is competent for safe solo (§ 61.87).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.87 — Solo requirements for student pilots

details.summary: The student’s authorized instructor administers the required pre-solo knowledge test (not a DPE or FSDO by default). Document the test and training before the solo endorsement.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.87 — Solo requirements for student pilots

details.summary: Pre-solo knowledge test must cover applicable regulations, flight characteristics, and operational limitations of the make/model to be flown (§ 61.87).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.87 — Solo requirements for student pilots

details.summary: Bank stem/answer look swapped. Pre-solo requires specific flight/ground training in § 61.87. Separately: each solo cross-country generally needs a logbook endorsement for that flight (with the limited repeated-route exception in § 61.93).

Yes — repeated solo cross-country flights without a new endorsement for each flight are authorized only under stipulated conditions in § 61.93 (same route, distance limits, prior dual both directions, etc.).

Solo XC authorization requires a logbook endorsement that the instructor reviewed preflight planning/preparation and the student is prepared to make that flight safely (plus the other § 61.93 endorsements).

Repeated solo XC over the same route without a per-flight endorsement: yes, if the route is no more than 50 NM from the departure point and instruction was given in both directions over the route (and other § 61.93 conditions).
Solo in Class B requires a logbook endorsement showing ground and flight instruction in that specific Class B airspace for which solo is authorized (§ 61.95 / § 61.87 as applicable).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.95 — Operations in Class B airspace and at airports located in Class B

details.summary: Only the flight instructor who conducted the Class B training may endorse the student for solo in that Class B airspace — not just any CFI on the field.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.95 — Operations in Class B airspace

details.summary: A Recreational Pilot Certificate may be issued for airplanes, gyroplanes, and helicopters — not for gliders (glider private/commercial paths are separate). Confirm category/class privileges in Part 61 Subpart D.
Minimum age for a Commercial Pilot Certificate is 18 years (14 CFR 61.123). Private is 17 for airplane/rotorcraft/glider; ATP is 23 (or 21 with restricted ATP paths).

Commercial Pilot Certificate — glider: among the experience paths, one common bank key is at least 25 hours in gliders and 100 glider flights as PIC (see current § 61.129 glider options — flight/hour combinations vary by launch method).

To prepare a glider applicant for an initial CFI certificate, the training instructor must have held a Flight Instructor Certificate for at least 24 months and given at least 80 hours of glider training (§ 61.195).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.195 — Flight instructor limitations and qualifications

details.summary: Each flight instructor must retain a record of the type and date of each student-pilot endorsement given for 3 years (§ 61.189).

Bank key: a flight instructor applying for an additional rating on that certificate must have a minimum of 5 hours as PIC in the category and class appropriate to the rating sought (as tested). Confirm the current § 61.183 / § 61.187 hour table for the specific rating when advising applicants — some airplane ratings require more.
In any 24 consecutive hours, an instructor is limited to 8 hours of flight training (§ 61.195). Plan dual schedules with this hard cap.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.195 — Flight instructor limitations and qualifications

details.summary: To endorse solo XC privileges, the instructor must determine that the student’s preparation, planning, and procedures are adequate for the proposed flight under existing conditions (§ 61.93).

To endorse a student for solo, the instructor must have given that student flight training in the type (make/model as required) of aircraft involved — you cannot endorse a ship you have not trained them in (§ 61.87).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.87 — Solo requirements for student pilots

details.summary: A Flight Instructor Certificate may be renewed by successfully completing a flight instructor refresher course (FIRC) within 3 calendar months prior to renewal (among other § 61.197 methods).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.197 — Renewal requirements for flight instructor certification

details.summary: An expired Flight Instructor Certificate may be exchanged for a new one by passing the appropriate practical test (§ 61.199). You cannot renew an expired CFI with only a FIRC.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.199 — Expired flight instructor certificates and reinstatement

details.summary: In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the PIC may deviate from any rule in 14 CFR to the extent required to meet that emergency (§ 91.3). Teach: declare when able, fly the ship first, then sort paperwork.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.3 — Responsibility and authority of the PIC

details.summary: Bank answer “24 hours” does not match the stem. Rule: under 14 CFR 91.17, you may not allow a person who appears to be intoxicated / under the influence to be carried in a civil aircraft — except a medical patient under proper care. Teach the passenger alcohol rule separately from the crew 8-hour / 0.04% rules.
Bottle-to-throttle: no person may act as a crewmember within 8 hours after consuming alcohol (also 0.04% BAC and “under the influence” rules) — 14 CFR 91.17.

14 CFR 91.17 prohibits acting or attempting to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft while having a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04 percent or greater by weight. Also barred: within 8 hours after consuming alcohol, while under the influence of alcohol, or while using any drug that affects faculties contrary to safety.

Operating limitations are found in the aircraft flight manual / approved manual material, markings, and placards — or any combination thereof (14 CFR 91.9). For gliders, that means POH/AFM pages plus cockpit placards (Vne, weight, weak-link, etc.).

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.9 — Flight manual, marking, and placard requirements

details.summary: Required preflight action for every flight (§ 91.103): become familiar with all available information, including runway lengths at airports of intended use (and takeoff/landing distance data). Weather briefing is part of “all available information,” but this item’s keyed answer is runway lengths.

The preflight action requirement to consider alternatives if the flight cannot be completed (§ 91.103) applies to any flight not in the vicinity of an airport — i.e., away-from-airport / cross-country flights need alternate planning thought.

PIC must ensure each person on board is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten seat belts (and shoulder harnesses when installed). Crew use rules and “before movement” fastening are in 91.107 — teach both briefing and use.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.107 — Use of safety belts / shoulder harnesses

details.summary: When two or more aircraft approach an airport to land, right-of-way belongs to the aircraft at the lower altitude — but that aircraft shall not take advantage of the rule to cut in front of or overtake another (§ 91.113).

When a glider and an airplane approach head-on at the same altitude, both give way to the right (14 CFR 91.113). Also remember: powered aircraft generally give way to gliders / balloons / airships in converging situations — but head-on is both right.

Over a congested area, 14 CFR 91.119 requires at least 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a 2,000-foot horizontal radius. Over other than congested areas the minimum is 500 feet AGL (with other caveats). Glider instructors still brief this for aerotow routes and XC.

Except for takeoff or landing, the minimum safe altitude anywhere is an altitude allowing, if a power unit fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface (§ 91.119). Congested-area/other minima also apply.

If you deviate from an ATC instruction in an emergency and are given priority, submit a detailed report within 48 hours if the ATC facility manager requests it (§ 91.123). Know the 48-hour clock separately from NTSB accident reporting.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.123 — Compliance with ATC clearances and instructions

details.summary: Alternating red and green light from the tower means exercise extreme caution. Steady green = cleared to land/takeoff (context-dependent); flashing red = airport unsafe; etc. Memorize the light-gun table.

Minimum certificate to enter Class B: a Student Pilot Certificate with the appropriate Class B endorsement (plus clearance/equipment rules). Higher certificates also work — the question asks for the minimum.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.95 — Operations in Class B airspace
14 CFR § 91.131 — Operations in Class B airspace

details.summary: For a glider above 10,000 feet MSL and more than 1,200 feet AGL, basic VFR visibility minimum is 5 SM (with 1,000 ft above / 1,000 ft below / 1 SM horizontal cloud clearance). Below those altitudes different Class E/G tables apply — know § 91.155.

Before flight, the aircraft must have aboard (among other required papers) an Airworthiness Certificate, Registration Certificate, and approved Airplane/Rotorcraft/Glider Flight Manual when required — classic ARROW teaching. Logbooks need not be in the aircraft; MEL applies only if one is issued for that aircraft.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.9 — Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements

details.summary: Between 12,500 and 14,000 feet MSL, required minimum flight crew may operate up to 30 minutes without supplemental oxygen; above 14,000 continuous use is required (§ 91.211). The bank keys 12,600 as inside that 30-minute band.

Acrobatic flight minimums under 14 CFR 91.303 include at least 1,500 feet AGL and 3 statute miles visibility (plus the other listed restrictions: not over congested areas, not in Class B/C/D/E surface areas without authorization, etc.).

Each occupant must wear an approved parachute when an intentional maneuver exceeds 30° nose-up or nose-down relative to the horizon (with the usual training/spin exceptions in 91.307). Brief this before intentional unusual-attitude demos.
The owner or operator is primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft in an airworthy condition (14 CFR 91.403). PIC still determines airworthiness before flight (91.7).
Compliance with Airworthiness Directives is the responsibility of the owner or operator. ADs are Part 39 rules — accomplish as specified before further flight unless an AMOC is approved.

Completion of an annual inspection and return to service is indicated by the appropriate entries in the aircraft maintenance records (signed by the authorized person). Stickers alone are not the legal record.

links.label: 14 CFR § 43.9 — Content, form, and disposition of maintenance records

details.summary: If an alteration or repair substantially affected flight operation, the aircraft records must show a test flight and approval for return to service by an appropriately rated pilot before passengers are carried (14 CFR 91.407). Maintenance signoff alone is not enough when ops were substantially affected.

An annual inspection is due by the end of the 12th calendar month after the month of the last annual. If last annual was July 12 this year, the next is due no later than July 31 next year — not July 12/13 next year.

If an aircraft has not had a 100-hour or annual within the preceding 100 hours of time in service, giving flight instruction for hire in that aircraft is prohibited. The 100-hour rule applies to aircraft used for hire / flight instruction for hire under § 91.409.

Doing a 100-hour inspection early (for example at 90 hours) does not create a 110-hour next interval. The next 100-hour is still due after 100 hours time in service from that inspection. Unused hours are not banked.

NTSB “serious injury” includes injuries that require hospitalization >48 hours, fractures (except simple finger/nose/toe), severe hemorrhages, nerve/muscle/tendon damage, internal organ injury, or second-/third-degree burns over >5% of the body. Tendon damage is one of the listed examples on the test.

Substantial damage (NTSB) adversely affects structural strength, performance, or flight characteristics and normally requires major repair or replacement of the affected component. Cosmetic damage alone is not substantial damage.

Immediate NTSB notification is required for listed incidents including flight control system malfunction or failure — even when it is not an “accident.” Know the § 830.5 incident list separately from the accident definition.

Accidents (and certain incidents) require immediate notification to the nearest NTSB field office. “Immediately” means without delay once you are able to notify — do not wait for the written report deadline.

links.label: NTSB — Report an Accident or Incident

details.summary: After an accident, the operator must file a written report within 10 days (49 CFR 830.15). Immediate phone/electronic notification is separate from the 10-day report.

links.label: 49 CFR § 830.15 — Reports and statements to be filed

details.summary: For an incident (not an accident), a written report to the NTSB is required only if the NTSB requests it. Still notify immediately when the incident is on the § 830.5 list.

links.label: 49 CFR § 830.15 — Reports and statements to be filed

details.summary: Winch tow: CG hook advantage over nose hook — glider is less likely to pitch up violently if the towline breaks (nose hook can pitch up hard on break). CG hook is preferred for ground launch.
Using a CG hook for aerotow tends to make the glider pitch up (CG hook is aft of the nose). Aerotow normally uses the nose hook; CG hook is for winch/auto.

A knot in a rope can cut tensile strength roughly in half — a 1,000 lb rope may be good for about 500 lb with a knot. For aerotow, inspect ropes/weak links and avoid knots in the load path; follow GFH / manufacturer practices.

Aerotow towline (weak link) minimum strength is 80% of the glider’s certificated gross weight: 0.80 × 1,040 = 832 lb. Maximum is generally twice gross weight unless the stronger-link-at-towplane exception applies (§ 91.309).

Nose swings left before going right on a right-turn entry = slipping entry: not enough right rudder for the aileron used. Fix: more rudder with the aileron so the nose tracks with the horizon into the turn (coordinated).

If the nose moves into the turn before the bank starts, rudder was applied too soon (or too much) relative to aileron. Teach simultaneous coordinated inputs: aileron + rudder together, not rudder leading the roll.
Nose-low in a steep turn: reduce bank first, then apply back elevator to restore pitch. Pulling first while steep only increases load factor and can accelerate the spiral / stall. Bank → then pitch.
To minimize side loads on the landing gear at touchdown, keep the longitudinal axis parallel to the direction of motion (no crab at touchdown — wing-low / slip method for crosswind).
Proper crosswind landing at touchdown: aircraft’s direction of motion and longitudinal axis both parallel to the runway (aligned, not crabbed).
Emergency downwind landing: expect faster groundspeed at touchdown, longer ground roll, and higher chance of overshooting the aim point. Pick a longer field and accept the energy.
On final, use a faster-than-normal IAS when turbulent conditions exist (gust factor / turbulence margin). Extra speed protects against sudden sink and control loss.
Students round out high when they focus on references that are too close or look directly down. Teach aiming-point / peripheral ground-rush references farther ahead.

links.label: Aviation Instructor’s Handbook — Landing common errors

details.summary: Focusing too far ahead on approach makes it hard to judge height — result can be a delayed flare and nose-first / firm touchdown. Balance near and mid-distance visual cues.

links.label: Aviation Instructor’s Handbook — Landing common errors

details.summary: Excessive airspeed on final normally results in floating in ground effect before touchdown. Teach energy management: correct approach speed early; do not dive at the aiming point and expect a short landing.

Misjudging sink rate on landing often causes ballooning — too much back pressure when sink is less than expected. Recover with a slight forward pressure / wait for the float to settle, then finish the flare.
Bank stem/answer look swapped (seatbelts vs landing attitude). Landing cue often tested: hold a constant landing attitude in the flare/roundout. Separately, seatbelt briefing/use is § 91.107.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.107 — Use of safety belts / shoulder harnesses

details.summary: Straight-and-level in a crosswind: establish a proper heading into the wind (crab) with coordinated controls — wings level, ball centered, heading that cancels drift. Do not hold aileron into the wind for cruise crab (that’s a slip).

Accelerated stall in a steep turn: in a slip the high wing stalls first; in a skid the low wing stalls first; in coordinated flight both wings stall together. Teach coordination as spin-prevention, not just “pretty ball.”

A slipping turn is likely when you increase the rate of turn without using rudder (or with insufficient rudder) — bank/turn rate ahead of yaw coordination. Ball goes to the inside; fix with rudder toward the ball / less bank.

Towplane choice for aerotow: match (among other factors) stall speeds so the towplane does not force the glider into a high-AOA / stall-risk regime on climb or in turbulence. Towplane too slow or too fast both create teaching problems.

Water ballast: keep it while thermals are strong so higher wing loading gives higher interthermal cruise speed; dump when thermals weaken so you can thermal efficiently at a lower wing loading / lower sink. Net goal: increase average cross-country speed.

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Water Ballast / Performance

details.summary: Long final glide into a strong headwind: fly about best L/D speed plus half the estimated headwind at altitude (penetration speed). Pure best L/D into a headwind leaves you short.

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Speed to Fly / Headwind

details.summary: Excessive aerotow slack: yaw the nose to one side with rudder while keeping wings level with ailerons to take up the slack smoothly — do not dive aggressively into the rope.

Releasing from aerotow while still in the low-tow position risks the tow ring / rope striking and damaging the glider after release (the rope can slap up into the nose or canopy area). Teach normal release from high-tow (or the POH-approved position), confirm clear, then release — and brief abort/rope-break procedures so students never “dive off” low-tow as a habit.

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Launches and Landing (Ch 7)

details.summary: Cannot-release signal → towplane fishtails: plan final in low-tow and land before the towplane; use no spoilers or wheel brake on the rollout until after the towplane touches down (so you do not overrun into the rope/towplane).
Auto launch pitch limits (classic bank): do not exceed about 15° at 50 ft, 30° at 100 ft, and 45° at 200 ft. Progressive pitch protects against early rope break / whip-stall.

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Auto / Winch Launch

details.summary: On auto tow, establish the maximum pitch attitude for the climb at about 200 feet AGL (after stepping through the lower pitch limits).

Auto tow in strong crosswind: position glider and towrope obliquely to the takeoff line on the downwind side of the tow vehicle so the initial pull aligns better and reduces weathervane/side-load problems.

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Auto Launch / Crosswind

details.summary: Bank keys “raise the nose” to increase airspeed on ground launch — that conflicts with usual pitch-for-airspeed teaching (lower nose → accelerate). Treat the key cautiously; GFH/practice: pitch down to gain speed, pitch up to climb/slow. Confirm against your POH/training syllabus.
Winch-launch pitch oscillations are most often from insufficient up-elevator (or porpoising corrections). Smooth, adequate pitch control and correct climb schedule reduce oscillations.

Steep wind gradient on base/final into the wind: if you do not keep adequate airspeed, expect undershoot of the aim point or a stall as wind decreases near the surface. Add margin and plan a higher approach speed in gradient/shear.

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Approach / Wind Gradient

details.summary: Rule of thumb for final: about 50% above the glider’s stall speed plus half the estimated windspeed. Example: Vs 40, wind 20 → ~40×1.5 + 10 = 70. Adjust for ship, density altitude, and turbulence — POH wins.

Strong thermal on final (swirling dust/leaves): close spoilers and increase airspeed to punch through the sink/shear on the edges and preserve energy for the landing. Do not open more drag in the sink.
Multiple gliders in one thermal: turn in the same direction as the first glider that entered. Opposite-direction circling is a collision hazard. Announce and look before joining.
Slope/ridge soaring: all reversing turns should be made into the wind, away from the slope — never turn toward the ridge into rising/closing terrain. Standard ridge-safety rule.
Passing through lift with no plan to work it: bank suggests minimum sink speed to take altitude quickly while straight. (XC MacCready practice may differ — teach the keyed FAA answer for the test.)

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Speeds to Fly

details.summary: Off-field landing: land uphill if possible, even if that means some downwind component — slope often matters more than light wind for rollout/stop. Still respect strong wind and obstacles.

Safe off-field landing odds improve when you hold an approach speed of at least ~50% above stall plus half the estimated wind — same rule of thumb as a normal final, with extra respect for unknown surface and gradient.

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that impairs judgment, coordination, and reaction time. It also reduces the body’s tolerance to hypoxia — a given altitude feels “higher” physiologically after drinking. Coffee does not metabolize alcohol faster; only time clears it. Teach the 8-hour bottle-to-throttle rule as a minimum, not a guarantee of fitness.
Upsloping terrain creates the illusion that the aircraft is higher than it actually is — pilots tend to fly too low on approach. Downsloping terrain does the opposite.

Spatial disorientation happens when the vestibular and proprioceptive senses conflict with what the eyes see — especially in IMC, night, or unusual attitudes. The recommended recovery is to ignore body sensations and rely entirely on the flight instruments (or a competent safety pilot / instructor on the gauges). Head movement reduction helps avoid vestibular illusions but is not the primary recovery procedure.

Haze makes traffic and terrain appear farther away than they really are — so you can be closer than your eyes suggest. Teach students to slow the scan assumptions and use ADS-B/radio as backups, not substitutes for seeing.

Teach a systematic empty-field scan: focus on different segments of the sky for short intervals rather than staring or continuously sweeping without focusing. Eyes need a moment to focus at each point to detect traffic.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Dark adaptation is impaired by cabin altitudes above about 5,000 feet (hypoxic effect on night vision). Also avoid bright white light before night flight.

As you climb, the percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere stays about 21% — partial pressure falls with total pressure. Hypoxia risk rises because fewer O₂ molecules are available per breath, not because the mix changes.

Hypoxia symptoms vary by person but commonly include euphoria, belligerence, a false sense of security, impaired judgment, headache, dizziness, tingling, and cyanosis. Nitrogen bubbles cause decompression sickness (the bends), not hypoxia. Concentration alone cannot overcome hypoxia — you need oxygen, lower altitude, or both.

Hypoxic hypoxia at altitude is caused by reduced barometric (atmospheric) pressure, which lowers the partial pressure of oxygen available to the lungs — even though the percentage of oxygen in air stays about 21%. The trap choice “decreasing amount of oxygen with altitude” confuses percentage with partial pressure. Teach students: same mix, less pressure, less O₂ molecules per breath.

Above about 15,000 feet without supplemental oxygen in an unpressurized aircraft, expect hypoxic signs such as cyanosis (blue lips/fingernails) and tunnel vision — plus impaired judgment. Use oxygen early; do not wait for symptoms.

Hyperventilation is abnormally rapid or deep breathing that blows off too much carbon dioxide (hypocapnia). Symptoms can mimic hypoxia (dizziness, tingling, visual disturbance). It is a CO₂ problem, not primarily an oxygen shortage — and increasing supplemental oxygen flow is not the fix.

Rapid or overly deep breathing while on oxygen commonly causes hyperventilation. Students may over-breathe when anxious or when first using a mask/cannula. Watch for lightheadedness and tingling; coach calm, normal-rate breathing rather than “more oxygen.”

To overcome hyperventilation: slow the breathing rate and restore carbon dioxide (breathe normally; historically, rebreathing into a paper bag was taught when hypoxia is ruled out). Do not speed up breathing. Distinguish hypoxia (need O₂ / descend) from hyperventilation (need slower breathing / more CO₂).

Smoking (and carbon monoxide exposure) reduces the blood’s oxygen-carrying capability by binding to hemoglobin — a form of hypemic hypoxia. It also degrades night vision. Teach smokers that physiological altitude is effectively higher and that CO plus altitude compounds risk.

At night, rods (off-center vision) detect dim objects better than cones (center). Force off-center viewing — look slightly to the side of where you expect the target — to increase night vision effectiveness.

For motion sickness in training: have the student minimize unnecessary head movement and keep eyes on a fixed outside reference (horizon). Closing eyes or looking down often worsens it. Avoid recommending medication that is not approved / that impairs performance; many anti-motion-sickness drugs are sedating.

links.label: Aviation Instructor’s Handbook — Student emotional reactions

details.summary: Motion sickness is caused by continued stimulation of the vestibular apparatus in the inner ear (the organs that sense balance and motion), especially when visual and vestibular cues disagree. Experience and smooth instruction help, but the mechanism is vestibular — not stomach acid.

ADM frames every aviation situation with four fundamental risk elements: Pilot, Aircraft, Environment, and External pressures (often taught as mission / external pressures — PAVE: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures). Instructors should have students score each element on every flight.

Introduce aeronautical decision making (ADM) as soon as the student can control the aircraft in basic maneuvers — not after solo, and not delayed until cross-country. Early ADM builds risk awareness while the student still has cognitive bandwidth once basic control is established. Keep ADM practical: identify hazards, assess risk, and mitigate during normal lesson tasks.

links.label: Aviation Instructor’s Handbook — ADM / Risk Management teaching
Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge — Aeronautical Decision-Making

details.summary: Realistic distractions during training flights check whether the student can maintain aircraft control while attention is diverted — a core divide-attention / workload skill. Distractions should be intentional teaching tools (radio calls, checklist interruptions, “passenger” questions), not unsafe overload. The goal is safe control first, then resume the interrupted task.
