links.label: Aviation Instructor’s Handbook — Teaching Methods / Flight Instruction

details.summary: Although not always required by regulation at that altitude, supplemental oxygen is recommended for night flight above about 5,000 feet — night vision is especially hypoxia-sensitive.

Altitude-chamber (or similar controlled hypoxia) training’s main advantage is that each pilot learns their own personal hypoxia symptoms in a safe, supervised setting. Symptom sets differ person-to-person; recognizing your pattern early is the teaching point — not merely watching others or relying on rapid chamber repressurization.

links.label: FAA Civil Aerospace Medical Institute (aeromedical education)

details.summary: Hypemic (“anemic”) hypoxia occurs when blood cannot carry enough oxygen — classic classroom example is carbon monoxide from a leaking exhaust system binding to hemoglobin. Symptoms resemble hypoxic hypoxia, but the cause is blood oxygen transport, not low ambient pressure. Treat with fresh air / oxygen and land; fix the exhaust leak on the ground.
Effective traffic-pattern collision avoidance: maintain the proper pattern altitude and continually scan. Altitude discipline keeps you predictable; scanning finds traffic early.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Most midair collisions occur during daylight in VFR conditions — often on clear days near airports/traffic patterns where traffic density is high. See-and-avoid never stops just because the weather is “nice.”

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Most effective night traffic technique: avoid staring directly at the suspected aircraft — use peripheral / off-center vision and a scanning pattern. Staring bleaches night vision on that spot and can make the target disappear.

FAA definition: Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM) is a systematic approach to the mental process used by pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances. It is more than “good judgment” alone — it is a structured process (DECIDE plus risk tools like PAVE/CARE).

Risk management within ADM reduces flight risk through situational awareness, problem recognition, and good judgment. Teach students to notice change early (SA), name the problem, then apply sound judgment and mitigation — not just memorize procedures after the fact.

One explicit step in the ADM process is identifying personal attitudes hazardous to safe flight. Before antidotes or DECIDE steps help, the pilot must know which hazardous attitude is driving the poor choice. Build this into debriefs: “Which attitude showed up today?”

Classic behavioral traps for experienced pilots: complete the flight as planned, please passengers, meet schedules, and “get the job done.” Call these out in ADM scenario training — mission completion pressure is a leading human-factor hazard.

Dangerous tendencies / behavior patterns called out in ADM training include peer pressure, get-there-itis / scud running, loss of situational awareness, and operating with inadequate fuel (or energy/options) reserves. Instructors should name these patterns in scenario training and require a mitigation before launch.

To get a realistic view of your attitude toward flying, take a Self-Assessment Hazardous Attitude Inventory Test (FAA ADM materials). It surfaces which of the five hazardous attitudes you lean toward so you can practice antidotes.

Classic hazardous attitudes include antiauthority (“don’t tell me”), impulsivity (“do it quickly”), and resignation (“what’s the use”) — along with macho and invulnerability. Know the five; this question samples three of them. Pair each with its antidote phrase in oral prep.

Hazardous attitudes are counteracted by an appropriate antidotal phrase (e.g., antiauthority → “Follow the rules. They are usually right.”; impulsivity → “Not so fast. Think first.”; invulnerability → “It could happen to me.”; macho → “Taking chances is foolish.”; resignation → “I’m not helpless. I can make a difference.”). Recognition alone is not enough — apply the antidote.

The five hazardous attitudes every pilot faces to some degree: antiauthority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, and resignation. Memorize all five and their antidotes for the FOI/ADM oral and written.

The first step in neutralizing a hazardous attitude is recognizing the hazardous thought when it appears. Only after recognition can the pilot apply the antidote and choose a safer action. Drill recognition in flight debriefs with concrete examples from the lesson.

When you recognize a hazardous thought: label it as hazardous, then correct it by stating the corresponding antidotal phrase — and act on the antidote. Recognition without the antidote leaves the bad attitude in charge.

Hazardous attitude — anti-authority: “The aircraft can handle a lot more than maneuvering speed.” Va (or design maneuvering speed) is a structural/control limit in turbulence and abrupt inputs; instructors must model respect for it, not dismiss it.
Antidote for the macho hazardous attitude (“I can do it / watch this”): “Taking chances is foolish.” Pair recognition with the antidote phrase, then choose the safer action.

Cockpit stress management starts before the crisis: assess stress areas in one’s personal life. Life stress carries into the cockpit and reduces spare mental capacity. Instructors should model go/no-go honesty when life stress is high (IMSAFE: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion/Eating).

At the first sign of cockpit stress, relax and think rationally — deliberate calm beats rushing into the next switch or control input. Teach a brief reset: breathe, prioritize aviate/navigate/communicate, then act. Avoid dumping unrelated life-stress analogies into the moment of the emergency.
Lines of longitude (meridians) cross the Equator at right angles and converge at the poles. Latitude lines are parallel to the Equator. This is basic chart geometry for true course measurement.

Measure true course on a sectional at a meridian near mid-route because meridians converge: the angle between your course and true north changes along the route. Midpoint measurement averages that convergence error.
Wind triangle (typical FAA figure): the line from A to B represents true heading and airspeed (the aircraft vector through the air). Know which leg is TH/AS vs TC/GS vs wind.
Wind triangle: line from C to B represents groundspeed and true course (the path over the ground). That is the course/GS vector you plot on the chart.
Wind triangle: line from C to A represents wind direction and velocity (from wind-dot to air-vector tip, depending on construction). Wind is from → to along that vector.

True course → magnetic heading: apply variation (add west / subtract east — “East is least, West is best”), then apply wind correction (subtract left WCA / add right WCA) to get magnetic heading. Sequence: TC ± var = MC, then ± WCA = MH.
Magnetic course → true course: add easterly variation (and subtract westerly). Going MC→TC is the reverse of TC→MC. Variation depends on location, not on which way the nose is pointed.
True heading → true course: remove the wind correction angle — subtract a right WCA (or add a left WCA). Heading is where the nose points; course is the path over the ground.
Magnetic variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north. It is printed on charts as isogonic lines and changes slowly over years — always use current chart variation.

Answer: 2 only. Bank wording “indication V2” means the sample instrument labeled V (letters T–Z under the gauges)—not a second instrument, and not the TO/FROM flag. Figure note: OBS is set to 180° (18 under the top index on every gauge; 030 at the bottom is only the reciprocal). Read instrument V as a whole: OBS 180 + that needle deflection + FROM. Then find which airplane around the compass rose would see that same picture—only aircraft 2. Airplane heading in the drawing does not change the CDI/TO-FROM; position relative to the station and the OBS setting do. Distractors (6 only; 5 and 8) are other positions that match different lettered indications.
VOR/OMNI figure item: indication U corresponds to aircraft position 6 only. Same method — resolve OBS setting, TO/FROM, and CDI deflection against each numbered position until only one fits.

VOR/OMNI figure item: aircraft 8 would show indication W. Work TO/FROM and left/right sensing from the aircraft’s position relative to the selected course; W is the unique match for that station geometry.

Sectional Figure 44: choose an altitude that stays under the Class B shelves between Northwest (area 2) and McKinney (area 5). Keyed answer is 2,500 feet MSL — read the blue Class B altitude boxes along the route and stay below the floor.

links.label: FAA Chart Users’ Guide — Class B

details.summary: Figure 44 obstruction 10 SM west of McKinney: charted obstruction heights — keyed that the top is 487 MSL or less for that symbol/group. Read the bold MSL number (and AGL in parentheses when shown) on the chart.

Figure 45, McCampbell (area 1): read where controlled airspace begins — keyed as 718 feet MSL for this chart set (often a Class E floor expressed with field elevation context). Always confirm the magenta vignette / chart notes on the figure.

links.label: FAA Chart Users’ Guide — Class E floors

details.summary: Figure 45 near Corpus Christi VORTAC (area 5): controlled airspace begins at 700 feet AGL (magenta vignette Class E transition area). Magenta = 700 AGL floor; soft blue = 1,200 AGL floor.

Figure 45, Bishop to McCampbell at 2,000 MSL: two-way radio is required when entering the Corpus Christi Class C airspace. Outside Class C/D/B, VFR radio may not be required — the trigger is penetrating that Class C.

Figure 45, Cuddihy (area 8): minimum avionics (with owner permission as the stem notes) are two-way radio and a Mode C transponder — because the airport sits in/under Class C / Mode C requirements for that chart area.
Figure 45, NAS Kingsville (area 2): airspace beginning at the surface is Class D (dashed blue airport traffic area). Military fields still use the same Class D depiction when a tower is operating.

Alert areas (Figure 45 area 6): no special clearance or equipment requirement, but pilots should be extremely cautious due to high-volume training. Participation is voluntary awareness — not a clearance regime.
Figure 46, Livermore Class D: the charted ceiling is 2,900 feet MSL (the number in the dashed-blue box). Class D tops are MSL altitudes on the sectional, not “2,500 AGL” by default.
Figure 46 over Hayward (area 3): Class B begins at 1,500 feet MSL per the blue altitude box for that sector. Fly below that floor (or get a clearance) to stay out of Class B.
Figure 46, San Jose Class C: the ceiling is charted at 4,000 feet MSL. Read the magenta Class C altitude stacks on the figure — surface/shelf floors and the top.

On a sectional (Figure 46), the large blue two-digit value like “2a” / MEF in a quadrangle is the Maximum Elevation Figure — highest terrain/obstacle elevation in that grid square, with a safety buffer, expressed in thousands/hundreds of feet MSL.

Figure 46, Gnoss to Rio Vista: use the highest Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) along the route for obstruction clearance planning — keyed 3,200 feet MSL. MEF is the large blue two-digit value in each quadrangle.

Class C outer area (area B on Figure 47) normally has about a 20 NM radius. Procedural ATC services are provided there when participation criteria are met; it is not charted like the Mode C veil of Class B.

A private pilot (ASEL) may act as PIC of an airplane towing a glider if, within the preceding 24 months, that pilot has made at least three flights as PIC of a glider towed by an aircraft (plus the other 61.69 requirements: endorsements, ground/flight training, etc.).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.69 — Glider towing: experience and training

details.summary: The runway/runway hold position sign (red with white runway numbers, often both directions) denotes intersecting runways — hold short of the intersection as directed.

Runway hold position markings on a taxiway (four yellow lines: two solid, two dashed) hold aircraft short of the runway. Solid lines on your side means do not cross without clearance (or CTAF discipline at nontowered fields).
An outbound destination sign identifies direction to takeoff runways (black background with yellow legend/arrow pointing toward the runway complex).
A taxiway location sign (yellow inscription on black background) identifies the taxiway you are on. Direction signs are black on yellow and point toward other taxiways/runways.
Elevators rotate the airplane about its lateral axis (pitch). Teach axes with controls: elevator → lateral, ailerons → longitudinal, rudder → vertical.
Ailerons rotate the airplane about its longitudinal axis (roll). Coordinate with rudder to manage adverse yaw.

Bank answer text looks swapped. True altitude is actual height above mean sea level (calibrated for nonstandard temperature/pressure). Indicated altitude is what you read on the altimeter with local setting.
Absolute altitude is height above the terrain/surface (AGL). Radar altimeters read absolute altitude; you estimate it visually or from chart elevation + true altitude.
Indicated altitude equals true altitude at sea level under standard conditions (when the altimeter setting and atmosphere match the calibration assumptions).
The pitot system supplies impact (ram) pressure to the airspeed indicator. Altimeter and VSI use static pressure only.
Figure 24: at pressure altitude 3,000 ft, raising temperature from 30°F to 50°F increases density altitude about 1,300 feet. Warmer air → higher DA.
Pressure altitude ≈ field elevation corrected for altimeter setting vs 29.92. For 3,563 ft and 29.96, keyed PA is 3,527 ft MSL (slightly below elevation because setting > 29.92).

If equipment has been added beyond original empty weight, allowable useful load decreases (max gross − new empty weight). Always use current empty weight/CG from the latest W&B sheet, not the old POH sample empty weight.

links.label: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook

details.summary: A runway exit sign indicates the designation and direction of an exit taxiway from the runway — helps you plan rollout exit without missing the turnoff.
Figure 30 wind component: landing Runway 18 with wind 220° at 30 kt → 40° off the nose. Crosswind ≈ 30 × sin(40°) ≈ 19 knots. Use the wind rose / component chart in the supplement.

High density altitude reduces climb performance (and lengthens takeoff/landing distances). Thin air = less lift and less propeller/engine performance for powered ships; for gliders, true airspeed and energy management change.
Pressure altitude is the altitude indicated when the altimeter’s barometric scale is set to 29.92 in Hg. It is the standard starting point for performance and DA calculations.
If density altitude is beyond chart capability, do not attempt takeoff until conditions allow calculations that show a safe takeoff and climbout. No guesswork past the chart.

Bank answer text looks swapped (airfoil axis wording). Concept for the stem: on older radar summary charts, an echo top like .250 with an underline coded the maximum top height band (tens of thousands of feet). Prefer modern GFA / radar mosaics on aviationweather.gov for current products, and learn the legend of whatever chart the test figure shows.
Public figures (VIP movement) are protected by Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs), often under § 91.141 / FDC NOTAMs. Check NOTAMs before every flight — stadium and VIP TFRs are common.
When changing squawk codes, avoid inadvertent selection of 7500 (hijack), 7600 (lost comm), and 7700 (emergency). Dial carefully through those codes; some panels let you preset then activate.

links.label: AIM 6-4 — Two-way Radio Communications Failure / Emergency codes

details.summary: The ILS critical area boundary sign identifies the edge of the ILS critical area. Do not enter beyond it when ATC protects the ILS (typically low ceilings/visibility) unless cleared.

links.label: AIM 2-3-5 — ILS Critical Area Markings / Signs

details.summary: Bank is mis-topic’d under systems (certificate renewal). Passing a flight instructor practical test in one category/class (e.g., single-engine airplane) renews the instructor certificate with its ratings for the renewal period — you do not need a separate ride in every rating to renew the whole certificate. Confirm current Part 61 renewal paths (FIRC vs practical test).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.197 — Renewal requirements for flight instructor certification

details.summary: Antidote for antiauthority (“don’t tell me”): “Follow the rules. They are usually right.” Say the antidote, then comply / choose the safer legal option.

Human behavior is cited as a factor in about three out of four accidents — the teaching point behind ADM, CRM, and risk management. Technical skill matters, but judgment and behavior dominate the accident record.

Bank answer text looks swapped (instrument wording). Concept: when turning onto a taxiway from another taxiway, a taxiway directional sign indicates designations/directions of taxiways leading out of the intersection (black legend on yellow) so you select the correct route.
METAR Figure 3 at KBRO: rain begin/end remarks give duration — keyed answer is 25 minutes for that observation. Practice decoding RAB/RAE pairs in the RMK section.

Student pilot certificate applications are submitted to an FSDO, an authorized flight instructor, or a designated pilot examiner (IACRA / in-person process as currently published). Plastic student certificates are issued by the FAA after processing.

Bank answer text looks swapped (instrument wording). Concept for the stem: from Hicks (area 1) northeast toward Northwest (area 2) on Figure 44, read the Class B floors and pick the maximum altitude that remains under the shelf — use the figure’s blue altitude boxes (same skill as bank_634).

links.label: FAA Chart Users’ Guide — Class B

details.summary: Figure 21 among aircraft 1–3: lowest aspect ratio is aircraft 1 (compute span÷chord). Low AR → more induced drag.

A forecast K-index of 35 implies a high likelihood of thunderstorms (commonly taught as about a 60% chance in FAA weather materials). Higher K → more unstable / moist mid-levels → better thunderstorm potential. Cross-check with outlooks, radar, and AIRMETs/SIGMETs.
After scuba diving without a controlled ascent, wait at least 12 hours before flight to cabin altitudes of 8,000 feet or less. Decompression sickness risk rises with altitude after diving.
After scuba diving that required a controlled ascent (decompression stop), wait at least 24 hours before flying to 8,000 feet or less. Longer waits apply for higher cabin altitudes.
K-index +17: expect good afternoon soaring with a chance of showers (moderate instability/moisture). Higher K → better thunderstorm potential; very high K is more storm than soar.
(Figure 8) On a Surface Analysis chart, symbol “12” denotes a squall line. Use the Figure pill; match the legend for fronts, troughs, and squall-line symbology.
Same solo-XC endorsement idea as bank_420: logbook endorsement that preflight planning/preparation was reviewed and the student is prepared to make the flight safely.
If the towplane releases while the glider is in low-tow, the rope can foul the glider’s nose, canopy, or flying surfaces. Prefer high-tow for release; brief rope-on-glider emergencies.

Extending flaps increases wing camber, which increases both lift and drag (for a given AOA/speed regime). That is why flaps allow slower approach speeds but also steeper approaches / more drag for path control.

Trigger temperature is the surface temperature needed for the surface parcel to rise through roughly the first 4,000 feet on a dry adiabatic lapse rate — i.e., when thermals start “triggering” deep convection for soaring.
Yellow demarcation bar marks the boundary between a runway with a displaced threshold and a blast pad, stopway, or taxiway that precedes the runway. Land beyond the displaced threshold markings.
A K-index of 10 indicates little or no thunderstorm potential (stable/dry enough that storms are unlikely). Contrast with K 30+ for high storm chances.
Same key idea as the other stability card: the most desirable stability is positive dynamic stability — disturbances damp out over time and the aircraft returns to equilibrium.

Gliders usually feel ground effect at less than about half the wingspan above the surface. Long-span ships therefore enter ground effect higher than short-span trainers — plan the roundout accordingly to avoid prolonged float.
Same marking purpose as bank_692: the yellow demarcation bar delineates a displaced-threshold runway from the preceding blast pad/stopway/taxiway.

Induced drag is the portion of total drag created by producing lift, and it changes a lot with airspeed (high at low speed). Duplicate of the core induced-drag teaching point — hammer it for the oral.

In a developed spin, load factor is typically low — about 0.5 to 1.5 G — not a high-G spiral. That is why “it doesn’t feel violent” can lull pilots; airspeed and turn rate still matter for recovery and structural limits after recovery.
Lift is the net force perpendicular to the relative wind — same definition card as bank_009. Keep drag parallel to relative wind; do not measure lift off the horizon.

This bank row is OCR-corrupt (broken id/stem/choices). Teaching point usually intended: moist air masses commonly bring poor visibility, stratiform clouds, and stable conditions compared with dry/continental air. Prefer a clean air-mass question from PHAK until this card is repaired in the import.

details.summary: A 100-hour inspection is required under 91.409(b) when the glider is carrying persons for hire (flight instruction for hire or paid sightseeing). An annual inspection is still required in addition to the 100-hour.

Club/demo sightseeing in a glider can avoid Part 119 because 119.1(e)(5) excepts nonstop commercial air tours in an airplane or glider that begin and end at the same airport and stay within 25 SM of the takeoff airport. Part 91.147 / Part 136 sightseeing rules do not apply to gliders, but 91.409(b) 100-hour inspection still applies when carrying persons for hire.

Under 61.129(f)(2), if you already have 200 hours in heavier-than-air aircraft, the commercial glider path requires 20 glider PIC flights; 3 hours dual (or 10 training flights) including 3 practical-test prep flights in the 2 calendar months before the test month; and 5 solo flights covering the 61.127(b)(6) areas of operation.

14 CFR 91.309: towline at least 200 ft; breaking strength 80–200% of glider max certificated operating weight. If the rope is stronger than twice MGW, install a glider-end safety (weak) link rated 80–200% MGW and a stronger towplane-end link (not more than 25% greater than the glider-end link and not more than 2× MGW).

Adding a glider category rating to an existing commercial airplane certificate generally does not require a new commercial knowledge test under 61.63. You still complete the commercial glider practical test using the additional-rating requirements in the PTS/ACS.

Airplane commercial → glider add-on required table: Navigation (VIII) is NONE. You typically also skip I.A Certificates, II.D Flight Deck Management, and III.A/C — but the evaluator may still sample skipped tasks, so prepare them.

Boxing the wake means maneuvering on tow in a rectangular pattern slightly outside the towplane’s wake while staying coordinated and in control (PTS IV.E). The Glider Flying Handbook cautions not to practice it below about 1,000 ft AGL.
PTS three-way exchange: “You have the flight controls” / “I have the flight controls” / “You have the flight controls,” followed by a visual check that the other pilot has the stick.
